Case Vignette: Rana (Age 55, HVAC Technician, Refugee Trauma)

Rana comes into the office with her shoulders pulled forward, a faint smell of solder and copper clinging to her denim shirt. She sits on the edge of the chair, hands folded tightly, eyes scanning the room once before settling on the floor. She says little at first, but when she does speak, her voice is low and careful, as if she is still learning which words are safe to say out loud.

She was born in a city in the Middle East where she worked as a seamstress and raised two daughters. Her husband disappeared during a period of sectarian violence when she was thirty-eight. She never learned what happened to him, only that one morning he left for the market and never came back. Three days later, a militia group forced its way into her home. They searched the rooms, smashed her sewing machine, and demanded to know where her husband was. One of them held a knife to her younger daughter's throat while Rana stood frozen. She remembers the smell of cigarette smoke and the sound of her own teeth chattering. They left after an hour, but the threat never left.

Within a week, she packed a bag and walked with her daughters across the border. They spent two years in a refugee camp in a neighboring country. She describes the camp as a place of open mud and closed futures. At night, the sounds of distant gunfire or even a dropped metal pan would send her heart into her throat. She learned to sleep with one eye open, to keep her daughters' shoes tied at all times. She began to flinch at the crackle of a plastic tarp in the wind.

When they were finally resettled in the United States, Rana was forty-three. She did not speak English, had no money, and had never touched a furnace. A caseworker helped her enroll in a vocational program for HVAC work because, as Rana puts it, "No one touches a woman who fixes their boiler." She learned the trade quickly-she liked the logic of valves and compressors, the predictability of pressure gauges. The work gave her a kind of control she had not felt since before her husband disappeared.

Now, twelve years later, she is a lead technician for a small company. She drives a rusted van full of copper tubing and refrigerant gauges. She is divorced-her second marriage, to another refugee, fell apart because she could not sleep in the same room with anyone. His snoring sounded too much like a generator in the camp.

In the last six months, her symptoms have worsened. She has nightmares nearly every night-not always about the soldiers, but about small, crushing things: a door that won't lock, a staircase that goes nowhere, the sound of a zipper opening too fast. She wakes up sweating, convinced she needs to run. She has started arriving late to jobs because she takes three different routes to each house, avoiding underpasses and alleys. If a truck backfires on the street, she drops her tools and stands still, hands shaking, until the sound fades.

Her avoidance is deep. She will not watch any news about the region where she was born. She has stopped calling her daughters because their voices remind her of the camp. When a customer's basement has a low ceiling and a concrete floor, she makes her apprentice go down instead. She tells herself it is about safety, but really it is the sensation of being trapped-a feeling she cannot separate from the memory of a room with no windows.

Her job performance has begun to slip. She double-checks her pressure readings three times because she cannot trust her own memory. A supervisor recently noted she had left a wrench on a rooftop and then could not recall climbing the ladder. She has lost eight pounds in two months because she cannot eat in public-the sight of a crowded restaurant kitchen makes her feel like she is back in the camp's food line, waiting for something that might never come.

Yesterday, she drove past a yellow truck that resembled the militia's vehicle. She pulled over, put her head on the steering wheel, and cried for twenty minutes. She tells me she is tired of being inside her own head. She wants the work to be enough. But the work is no longer a sanctuary-it has become another place where the past shows up, uninvited.
